how-much-to-charge-to-stain-a-deck.html.text:
← Deck staining bid calculator

How much to charge to stain a deck

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$2.50 per square foot” special. That number is not a takeoff. A 200-square-foot platform with no rail is not the same job as a 192-square-foot 12x16 with 40 lineal feet of picket rail and a stair run. The trip is the same. The stainable surface is not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the rails and the stairs, not just “square feet of deck”

Deck-build calculators price posts, joists, and railing as construction. Exterior house painting prices elevations. A stain is a different job: the walking surface, the picket rail (both sides), the stairs, the prep, the coats, and the extras that are not in the coupon. Quoting all of that from a published per-square-foot special is how the first stair eats the field margin.

A job with the same trip can cost much more

Each lineal foot of picket rail is stainable surface that never appears on the coupon. Stairs, strip, a second coat of oil, and a second-story carry are billed as their own hours. On the sample rates a 192-square-foot 12x16 with 40 lineal feet of pickets, one stair, a wash, and two oil coats prices about $2,134.62 (14.1 crew-hours, $11.12 / walking sf). The same shop’s 200-square-foot platform hang prices about $631.88 (3.8 hours, walk-away $454.95, $3.16 / walking sf).

Matching the $2.50 / sf special is only about $45 above walk-away on the platform hang ($500 against a $455 walk-away), and it loses about $1,057 on the picket-rail oil job whose walk-away is already $1,536.93.

A strip-and-oil second-story is not automatically a markup on the platform

A 400-square-foot second-story deck with 80 lineal feet of pickets, two stairs, peeling-stain strip, two oil coats, and furniture is not the platform special plus 15%. On the sample rates that job prices about $6,688.21 (56.0 crew-hours). A 300-square-foot composite clean-and-seal with 50 lf of rail and one stair prices about $1,303.28 (9.7 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first stair.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $38/h painter loaded at 30% payroll burden is $49.40. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number. Zero walking feet still prices: stain hours are the surface, not an error. Picket rail defaults to 9 stainable square feet per lineal foot.

What this is not

This is not a construction specification, a coating warranty, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. The walking surface, the rail lineal feet, the stairs, the prep, the finish, and the access are yours to confirm. It does not price a new deck build, an exterior house paint job, or a hardwood-floor refinish.

Price your deck stain

Common questions

How much to charge to stain a deck?

Charge from the trip, the prep, the stainable surface (walking square feet plus rail lineal feet times stainable square feet per foot plus stairs), the coats, the access path, furniture, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 200-square-foot platform with no rail, a wash, and one water-based coat, at the sample rates in this calculator, prices around $632 (3.8 crew-hours, $3.16 per walking square foot).

Why is a $2.50 per square foot deck-stain special dangerous?

Homeowners count walking-surface square feet. Picket rails and stairs are stainable surface that do not scale with that number. Matching a cheaper special written for a platform is how a 12x16 with 40 lineal feet of pickets becomes a two-day loss. On the sample rates the $2.50 special ($500 on 200 sf) is only about $45 above the $455 walk-away on the platform hang, and it loses about $1,057 on the 192 sf picket-rail oil job whose walk-away is already $1,537.

How much to charge to stain a deck with picket rails and stairs?

A 192-square-foot 12x16 with 40 lineal feet of picket rail (360 extra stainable sf at 9 sf per foot) and one stair is 592 square feet of stain work, not 192 square feet of deck. On the sample rates a wash plus two oil coats prices around $2,135 (14.1 crew-hours, $11.12 per walking square foot), while a platform special hang prices around $632 (3.8 hours). A 400-square-foot second-story strip-and-oil job with 80 lf of pickets, two stairs, and furniture prices around $6,688 (56.0 hours).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not construction, legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

FOR DECK STAINING CREWS

Bid the rails, the stairs, and the coats.

Price a stain or seal the way the trade actually loses money: stainable surface from picket rails and stairs, strip versus wash, oil two-coat versus water, and second-story carry as their own hours. You get the bid, the hours the first picket rail actually consumes, and the walk-away number below which the job loses money.

The deck

Start from a common job, then replace every figure with your takeoff. Changing prep, finish, or access never overwrites a rate you already typed. This prices a stain — not a new deck build, and not a house paint job.

Your crew rates

A $38/h painter loaded at 30% is $49.40. Quoting the raw wage on a published $2.50/sf special is how a 12x16 with picket rails that looked fine turns into a two-day loss after the first stair. Zero walking feet still prices — stain hours are the surface, not an error. Picket rail defaults to 9 stainable sf per lineal foot (both sides of the pickets plus the rails).

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard or a coating warranty — replace them with your own takeoff.

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

      Common questions

      Why can a competitor advertise “$2.50 a square foot”?

      Usually because the special is written around one specific job, and that job is a preset here: a 200 sq ft platform with no rail, wash-only prep, and one coat of water-based stain. It really does price low. What the per-square-foot number cannot see is rail, stairs, prep level, coat count, and second-story access. Price your actual deck beside the special and the gap becomes a list of line items instead of an argument about who is honest.

      Why does 40 linear feet of picket rail add so much time if it isn’t walking-surface square footage?

      Because rail is stainable surface even though it is not deck square footage. A picket rail has far more surface area per linear foot than the flat decking it sits beside — every spindle has four sides to brush — so it is priced separately from the deck square footage rather than folded into it. Stair runs are treated the same way for the same reason: risers, treads, and stringers are surface a flat-sqft number never sees.

      What is the real cost difference between “wash only” and “strip peeling stain”?

      About 5× the labor and 7× the material. A wash-and-brighten starts at 0.55 hours and $3.50 of material per 100 sq ft. A wash-and-sand starts at 1.35 hours and $6. Stripping failed, peeling stain before washing and sanding starts at 2.7 hours and $24 per 100 sq ft — because old finish has to come off before the new coat has anything sound to bond to.

      Can I stain a composite deck the same way as a wood deck?

      No. Composite decking does not absorb a wood stain the way real lumber does, so the finish preset for composite is a clean-and-seal service rather than a stain, with its own coverage and hours starting point. Selecting composite as the finish is what tells the calculator to price the cleaning service instead of a stain job — picking “oil” or “water” on a composite deck would price a job that doesn’t match what actually happens on that material.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage so it is still here next visit, “Copy share link” encodes your inputs into this page’s own URL hash so a partner or the office can open the same bid, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your deck size, wages, or prices.

      What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

      The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — prep, coats, rail, stairs, access, and a furniture move — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all. Typing a price you are considering shows you the margin or the loss before you send it.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Deck Staining Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per square foot

"$2.50 a square foot" is not a price for a deck-staining job — it is a price for one specific deck, with no rail, no stairs, and ground-level access, quietly applied to every deck that calls in.

What a flat rate per square foot is

A flat rate per square foot is the fastest way to quote: multiply the deck's walking surface by a number and read off a price. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a homeowner holding a coupon or a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one deck — a bare platform, no rail, no stairs, ground level, a light wash — and then reused for every deck afterward, whether or not the next deck looks anything like the platform the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the walking surface, rail lineal feet, stair runs, prep method (wash, sand, or strip), finish (water, oil, or a composite clean-and-seal), access (ground or second-story), and whether furniture has to move, plus your own labor hours and material costs. It prices the whole stainable surface — deck, rail, and stairs — separately by task, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this job, not a generic one.

What a flat rate per square foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/sq ft whether the deck has a picket rail or none at all — even though rail is stainable surface that takes prep and coats just like the deck boards. Converts rail lineal feet to stainable square feet (9 sq ft per lineal foot, shipped default), so a railed deck costs more than a bare platform of the same walking surface.
Has no line for stair runs, regardless of how many the deck has or how much surface each one adds. Prices stair runs at a stainable square footage per run (40 sq ft, shipped default), so a deck with stairs costs more than the same walking surface with none.
Prices the walking surface alone, with no separate line for prep method — a wash and a full strip cost the same per square foot. Prices wash, sand, and strip at their own hours and material per 100 sq ft, so a peeling deck that needs a strip costs more than one that only needs a wash.
Has no line for second-story staging or a furniture move, regardless of whether the deck needs either. Prices second-story access hours and a furniture-move fee directly, so an elevated deck with furniture to shift costs more than a ground-level deck with none.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat rate would have quoted the same job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two decks, the same surface-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets and shipped shop rates ($38/hr crew wage, 30% burden, $75 travel and equipment, 15% overhead, a 28% target margin):

JobThis calculator's priceA flat $2.50/sq ft rate, applied by walking surface aloneGap
200 sq ft platform, no rail, no stairs, wash, 1-coat water, ground level (the job the $2.50/sq ft special was built on)$631.88 bid price; $454.95 break-even cost$500.00The flat rate clears this job's break-even cost by $45.05, but is $131.88 short of the calculator's own target-margin price.
400 sq ft deck, 80 lf picket rail, 2 stair runs, strip, 2-coat oil, second story, furniture move (1,200 sq ft of actual stainable surface)$6,688.21 bid price; $4,815.51 break-even cost$1,000.00The flat rate quotes $3,815.51 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $5,688.21 below the calculator's bid price.

Both flat-rate quotes apply the $2.50/sq ft rate to the deck's walking-surface square footage alone (200 and 400 sq ft), the way a per-square-foot special is normally quoted. The second job's actual stainable surface -- deck, rail, and stairs together -- is 1,200 sq ft, three times its walking-surface number, which is exactly what a flat rate per square foot cannot see. Run your own deck's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied past the one deck it was built for, and nothing about a per-square-foot number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per square foot get a deck-staining quote wrong?

Because the cost driver is stainable surface, not walking-surface area. Picket rails and stair runs are surface that has to be prepped and coated just like the deck boards, but a flat per-square-foot rate is almost always quoted off the walking surface alone -- the number on a tape measure or a listing, not the number a brush actually covers.

What does a flat rate usually leave out entirely?

Rail lineal feet, stair runs, second-story staging, and furniture moves. A 400 sq ft deck with 80 lf of picket rail and two stair runs has roughly three times the stainable surface of its walking-surface number alone, before second-story access or a furniture move add any hours at all -- and a per-square-foot rate has no line for any of it.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at the shipped shop rates: a 200 sq ft platform with no rail -- the job the $2.50/sq ft special was built on -- costs $454.95 to complete, so the $500 flat quote still clears cost, just $131.88 short of this calculator's own $631.88 target-margin price. Apply the same $2.50/sq ft to a 400 sq ft deck with 80 lf of picket rail, two stair runs, a strip prep, two-coat oil, second-story access, and a furniture move, and the $1,000 flat quote is $3,815.51 below that job's own $4,815.51 break-even cost -- before a dollar of profit.

Is a flat rate per square foot ever the right way to quote?

For a bare platform with no rail, no stairs, ground-level access, and a light wash -- the one job the rate was built on -- a flat rate can land close. The risk is applying it past that one job without noticing, because the rate is quoted off the walking surface and nothing on a tape measure says how much rail or stair surface the next deck is hiding.

Does this calculator know what stain or labor costs in my market?

No. It has no data on local material or labor rates. It takes the walking surface, rail lineal feet, stair runs, prep method, finish, access, and furniture moves, plus the labor hours and material costs you enter, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

vs-joist.html.text:
← Deck Staining Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Joist

Two different shapes: Joist is an account-based estimating, invoicing, and payment app for running a contractor's whole business. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one deck-staining job cost, given its stainable surface, rail, stairs, prep, and coats, before you write the estimate.

What each tool is for

Joist is estimating, invoicing, and payment-collection software, founded in 2011 and headquartered in Kelowna, British Columbia, Canada, later acquired by ServiceTitan in 2021. It is built for small contractors across trades — painters, remodelers, landscapers, deck builders — covering line-item estimates, branded proposals, signed approvals, invoicing, and in-app payment collection across a whole business, with a mobile app for use on site. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across every job, not a one-off calculator. Joist's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — estimating and invoicing software serving small contractors including deck-staining crews, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Joist appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Joist does. It does not build a branded proposal, collect a signature, or take a card payment, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one deck-staining job's walking-surface square feet, picket-rail lineal feet, stair runs, prep level — wash-and-brighten, wash-and-sand, or strip peeling stain — finish — water, oil, or composite clean-and-seal — coat count, second-story access, and a furniture move, plus loaded painter wage, payroll burden, travel and equipment, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the price, the price per walking square foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Is the price I'm about to quote still above my walk-away cost for this job?This calculator's walk-away price check.
I need to turn an accepted price into a branded, signable estimate and collect a deposit online.Joist — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.

Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Joist is used through a subscription account.

Most deck-staining crews get different value from each: Joist (or a comparable estimating app) for turning an accepted price into a branded proposal, signature, and payment as an ongoing subscription, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one deck should cost from its rail, stairs, prep, and coats before a business system is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a signed estimate, an invoice, or a payment record.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Joist?

They do different jobs, and a deck-staining crew of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. Joist, founded in 2011 and headquartered in Kelowna, British Columbia, Canada, is estimating, invoicing, and payment-collection software built for small contractors, acquired by ServiceTitan in 2021, sold as an ongoing subscription account. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from walking-surface square feet, picket-rail lineal feet, stair runs, prep level — wash, sand, or strip — finish, coat count, second-story access, and a furniture move, plus loaded painter wage, payroll burden, travel and equipment, overhead, and target margin, it turns that into the price, the price per walking square foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, before any of it touches a business-management system. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A deck-staining crew that already tracks estimates, invoices, and payments across every job is better served by Joist or a comparable estimating app; a contractor who wants an instant, private answer to what one deck should cost from its rail, stairs, and coats before opening a business system is in the right place here.
